There are two totally different stories floating around in AI right now, but they cannot both be true.

In one, AI memory is the hottest commodity on Earth. Samsung made ~$80 billion in Q3 operating profit, 99% from its chip division. @MicronTech  expects memory supply to get even tighter in 2027 and 2028.  

Meanwhile, viral videos are claiming a new @Stanford paper – Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) – ended LLMs and made NVIDIA's memory chips unnecessary.

Who is right?

I read the NCM paper to find out. In short, Stanford and Together AI proposed a new approach to text generation alongside autoregression and diffusion. NCM works like an architect: it sketches an outline first, then builds the structure, and only then cleans up the phrasing.

Instead of predicting the next token left to right, it predicts the next scale. The scales go from coarse to fine, but NCM samples all the codes within each scale in parallel. Changing just two early codes is enough to alter the characters and plot.

It turns out, that can make GPUs “happier.” 

I recorded this video to show you how NCM works and where it comes from, what it could change about how GPUs use memory, why this approach works so well on Sudoku, and why the speed gains over diffusion don’t tell us whether it’s faster than optimized LLMs. 

What excites me is that the more papers like this we read together, the less it looks like any one approach will replace all the others.

Looping is officially a trend now

1. Hot release – GLM-5.4, @Zai_org's first Loop Transformer.
Loops 28 mid-layers of the GLM-5 base twice, at 750B scale, and claims 2T–3T-class intelligence. Per-token gates control how much Pass 1 writes before Pass 2 refines, and the extra loop runs on a 128-token KV window, not the 1M cache.

2. Friday release: @thinkymachines' Inkling 2 Mini, a looped transformer you can run on a laptop.
24 layers total: middle 12 repeat 3 times, the first and last 6 run once. That gives 48 layer passes per token from 24 layers of weights. 26.4B params (3.4B active), ~5.4B weight activations per token, ~20GB, open weights.

3. Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers by @OuYoungXuan et al.
Save each layer's update on its own, cap total growth with geometric decay, and use attention to pick which past updates matter. Beats full-sized models with up to 60% fewer parameters.

4. Looped Weight-Space Programming, from @MBZUAI
Claude Opus 5.5 writes every weight of a small looped transformer by hand, with no training. One block repeats one step as long as needed.
It set 19,936 weights for $19 and solves 100% of Maze-Hard. A 928-weight version hits 100%, 1,900× fewer weights than LDT.

5. Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
It learns an energy over latent states, treats each loop as gradient descent on that energy, and uses the gradient to stop. With 1.8M parameters, it hits 99.9% on Sudoku-Extreme with 345× less inference compute than the next-best model.

Almost three years to the week after Sam Altman's five-day exile from OpenAI in November 2023, the AI industry ran the same experiment at roughly ten times the financial scale. And got the exact same answer.

What does it take to build a robot agent?

We have VLAs and WAMs as foundation models for robots. But we still haven't cracked real autonomy.

Digital agents use a harness, connecting models with memory, tools, planning, etc. So what if we make the harness embodied and pair it with VLAs or WAMs?

▪️ Grid Robotics proposed this idea as a blueprint for agentic robotics

Their framework has 3 layers:

- S2: foundation model + embodied harness. 
It's a decision center that interprets the goal, picks skills and tools, and checks outcomes
- S1: callable skills – VLA or WAM policies, object detection, motion planning, navigation
- S0: real-time body control – joints, balance, trajectory tracking

The S2 level is the most interesting for us now.

→ Foundation models provide knowledge and reasoning.
→ The embodied harness supplies everything around a model. It's basically an agent harness that works in the physical world.
It takes on the roles of context manager, tool and skill interface, planner, memory, and verifier. 
It determines what info reaches the model and what it can act on, how the system follows through on its decisions, and it maintains plans and memory.

Do you know what connects Jakub’s proposal to a guessing game Claude Shannon ran in 1951?

Shannon asked people to guess the next letter in a piece of text. How many guesses it took helped him estimate how predictable English was. In the 1970s, Fred Jelinek’s team at IBM used a related measure, perplexity, to describe how hard a speech recognition task was.

What I find fascinating is that Jakub is still asking how well you can predict what comes next. This time, he wants the answer to help AI labs decide when to slow down.

The best piece of advice from @simonw for everyone building software - go weird!

I’m so happy I got to interview Simon Willison. We talked about evals and software engineering in the age when he can build in an hour what used to take him a week.

That’s made him change his ambitions drastically. 

But I didn't expect to hear what he hopes to build next. For me, as a professional journalist, it felt so close: he wants to build tools that help local reporters find stories in data they might not have the resources to dig through on their own.

“My goal is for someone to win a Pulitzer Prize using my software for perhaps 3% of what they did. I want to contribute a tiny piece to Pulitzer-winning reporting, ideally at a newspaper that can’t afford software developers.”

If you’re into software engineering and AI evals, Simon is one of the first people I’d listen to. We also talked about how he handles the hard decisions AI leaves him with, how he decides which new models are worth trying, and why it’s easier than it used to be to build a benchmark around the work you actually do. And overall, he is just a pleasure to talk to.

The week in AI, by the numbers:

1. 250,000+ pages – the unpublished prose version of Levent Alpöge's claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis (and the Generalized RH), found with Claude in about 6 weeks. He posted only the Lean code, and the independent check is still running. Hours later, a 940-page all-human GRH draft came out too. Neither is verified yet.
2. $93.5B – Anthropic's IPO, the largest ever, at $83 a share. $81.3B at pricing, the rest from the underwriters' extra shares, closed today.
3. $5B – Isomorphic Labs' Series C, six months after its $2.1B round.
4. 46.2% – Gemini 4 Neon on @cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, about a point behind Opus 5.5 (47.3%) at about a third of the cost: $4.38 vs $12.82 per task.
5. 14% – the best PPA gain OpenAI's models found on AMD's flagship GPU design. Roughly a year of progress in under 5 months.
6. $8 / $40 – GPT-6.2 Astra per 1M tokens. Sol: $2 / $10.
7. 770B / 49B active – Hy4, now open weights, natively multimodal, 1M context. Hy4 flash: 224B / 12B.
8. 26.4B / 3.4B active – Inkling 2 Mini from @thinkymachines, open weights, ~20GB, runs on a 32GB Mac.
9. ~1 exabyte a month – the models and datasets Hugging Face now distributes.
10. 936 – studies by 936 AI agents from 35 labs in 12 weeks, as @askalphaxiv opens its preprint server to AI-written papers.
